prompt: A cyclist finishes a long summer ride without a water bottle. Put the moments of drive theory in order, from the first to the last.

steps.text: Before the ride, the cyclist's body is in a balanced physiological equilibrium.
steps.explanation: Drive theory starts from homeostasis, the balanced state the organism tries to keep.

steps.text: Hours of heat and effort leave the cyclist dehydrated, so homeostasis is disrupted.
steps.explanation: A biological need appears when the body moves away from equilibrium.

steps.text: An unpleasant feeling of thirst builds and pushes the cyclist toward a drink.
steps.explanation: The need produces a drive, an unpleasant internal state of arousal.

steps.text: The cyclist stops at a corner store and buys a bottle of water.
steps.explanation: Behavior is the effort to reduce the internal tension.

steps.text: After drinking, the thirst fades until the next long ride.
steps.explanation: Once consumption restores equilibrium, the drive subsides until the need recurs.

prompt: Each consumer below has stopped using a product. Which expectancy theory component has failed?

cases.text: A traveller quits a language app because he doubts that daily practice will ever make him fluent.
cases.explanation: He doubts that effort will lead to successful performance, so expectancy has failed.

cases.text: An accountant passes an online data course with top marks but sees that employers in her field ignore the certificate.
cases.explanation: Performance was achieved, but she no longer believes it leads to the outcome, so instrumentality has failed.

cases.text: A runner is sure the training plan would get him to a marathon finish line, and that finishing would earn a medal, but he does not care about medals.
cases.explanation: Effort and performance both look effective, but the outcome holds little value for him, so valence has failed.

cases.text: A retiree buys a keyboard to learn piano but cancels the lessons after deciding her stiff hands could never play a full song.
cases.explanation: She believes effort will not produce performance, which is a failure of expectancy.

cases.text: A shopper reaches the gold tier of a store program, then learns gold members receive no better prices than anyone else.
cases.explanation: Reaching the tier does not lead to the expected outcome, so the instrumentality link is broken.

prompt: Which kind of need is each purchase mainly meant to satisfy?

cases.text: After a power outage, a family buys bottled water and blankets to get through the night.
cases.explanation: Water and warmth are innate physiological requirements for sustaining life.

cases.text: A new manager joins an exclusive golf club mainly so colleagues see her as successful.
cases.explanation: Status and achievement are psychogenic needs, acquired by becoming a member of a culture.

cases.text: A shopper chooses a chest freezer by comparing storage capacity and yearly energy use.
cases.explanation: Storage capacity and energy use are objective, tangible attributes.

cases.text: A couple books a candlelit spa evening for the scents, warmth, and sense of escape.
cases.explanation: Sensory pleasure and fantasy are subjective, experiential benefits.

cases.text: A night-shift nurse buys blackout curtains so she can sleep during the day.
cases.explanation: Sleep is a physiological requirement.

cases.text: A student buys front-row concert tickets for the thrill of the live show.
cases.explanation: Excitement and sensory pleasure are hedonic needs.

prompt: Match each level of Maslow's hierarchy with the purchase that most directly serves it.

pairs.match: A hiker buys trail mix and an electrolyte drink before a long climb.
pairs.explanation: Food and water serve the physiological needs at the base of the hierarchy.

pairs.match: A new parent installs a smoke detector and buys home insurance.
pairs.explanation: Physical security and insurance serve safety needs.

pairs.match: A newcomer to the city joins a weekly running club to make friends.
pairs.explanation: Friendship and community clubs serve belongingness and love needs.

pairs.match: A chef pays for a prestigious culinary award entry to gain recognition from peers.
pairs.explanation: Prestige, mastery, and recognition serve esteem needs.

pairs.match: A retired engineer enrols in a pottery course to express himself creatively.
pairs.explanation: Creative expression and personal growth sit at the apex as self-actualization.

prompt: Which motivational conflict does each consumer face?

cases.text: With one bonus cheque, an employee would love both a new laptop and a road bike but can afford only one.
cases.explanation: Two desirable alternatives compete under one budget.

cases.text: A buyer loves a sports car's speed and looks but dreads its insurance premiums.
cases.explanation: One option carries both an attractive outcome and an undesirable outcome.

cases.text: A patient with a cracked tooth must choose between a costly crown and living with ongoing pain.
cases.explanation: Both alternatives carry a negative consequence.

cases.text: A shopper wants a slice of chocolate cake but feels guilty about the sugar.
cases.explanation: The same product attracts through taste and repels through health guilt.

cases.text: A student with a shattered phone screen must either pay for an expensive repair or keep using a phone that cuts her fingers.
cases.explanation: Each available option is undesirable.

cases.text: A couple with one free evening is torn between a new sushi bar and their favourite Italian bistro.
cases.explanation: Both options are attractive, and time allows only one.

prompt: Each person below is acting for a reason. Sort each case by whether the motive is intrinsic or extrinsic.

cards.text: A hobbyist answers beginners' questions on a camera forum because she enjoys helping them take better photos.
cards.explanation: She acts for the prosocial meaning and enjoyment of the activity itself.

cards.text: A shopper completes a store survey only to collect 500 loyalty points.
cards.explanation: The motive is an external contingency separated from the activity.

cards.text: A home cook posts recipes online for the pleasure of sharing what he makes.
A diner rates a restaurant app because every rating enters him in a prize draw.
cards.explanation: A sweepstakes entry is an external reward for the behavior.

cards.text: A buyer registers her new blender online to claim a 20-dollar cash rebate.
cards.explanation: A cash rebate is an outside reward, not part of the activity.

cards.text: A hiker posts a trail condition report so the next hikers know the bridge is out.
cards.explanation: Helping fellow hikers make informed choices is a prosocial, intrinsic motive.

prompt: Which source of involvement explains why each consumer is paying close attention?

cases.text: A shopper who normally grabs any bottle of wine spends twenty minutes choosing one to bring to his new manager's dinner.
cases.explanation: The gift occasion is a temporary contextual factor that raises involvement.

cases.text: A musician who sees herself as a serious guitarist always researches strings and amplifiers in depth.
cases.explanation: The category is central to her self-identity, which is enduring product involvement.

cases.text: A listener who skips most ads stays to hear a story-driven podcast ad for a bank all the way through.
cases.explanation: The narrative style raises his motivation to process the communication.

cases.text: A traveller compares airline seats carefully because the gate closes in ten minutes and the last flight is nearly full.
cases.explanation: Acute time pressure in this purchase situation raises involvement.

cases.text: A collector follows every review of luxury watches because the items are expensive and socially visible.
cases.explanation: Expensive, socially visible categories carry high enduring product involvement.

cases.text: A shopper scrolls through every panel of an interactive online ad for running shoes, reading each one.
cases.explanation: The media format draws the consumer into processing the message.
